headline: Arnold Clavio files cyberlibel vs. Zaldy Co’s alleged bodyguard
snippet: Veteran Kapuso broadcaster Arnold “Igan” Clavio has filed a cyberlibel complaint against Mario Ceniza Jr. over allegations that he received money linked to anomalous flood control projects. Clavio personally filed the complaint before the Quezon City Prosecutor’s Office on Wednesday, Oct. 14, accompanied by his lawyers. In an Instagram post, Clavio said he was taking legal action to defend his name and credibility, stressing that he stood by the truth. “Today, I stand for the truth,” Clavio wrote. “In filing this cyberlibel case, I stand firm in defending my name and credibility” (Sa paghahain ko ng cyberlibel case, naninindigan akong ipaglaban ang aking pangalan at kredibilidad). “Today, the truth will be triumphant,” he added, thanking GMA Network and his supporters for their trust. The complaint stemmed from allegations made by Ceniza, who reportedly identified himself as a bodyguard of former House Speaker Zaldy Co during a June 2026 press conference organized by former Anakalusugan party-list representative Mike Defensor. During the event, Ceniza accused several personalities, including media figures and celebrities, of allegedly benefiting from the supposed flood control project scam. He also named Clavio, claiming he had delivered cash to the broadcaster in a brown paper bag. Clavio has denied the allegation. Clavio said his decision to file the complaint was not intended to seek revenge against Ceniza but to address what he described as disinformation that had seriously damaged his name and reputation.

headline: Turning Cooked Rice into a Crisp Vessel for a Cold Fish Filling
snippet: Chef's note: The structure of this dish relies on the transformation of cooked rice into a rigid, edible vessel. It is a rice cake, not a pastry, but the critical variable is the same: how heat changes a soft, starchy mass into a crisp shell capable of holding a wet filling without collapsing. The recipe uses 240 g of cooked rice, divided into three thin discs, topped with 80 g of hard cheese, and baked at 180 °C for 18-20 minutes until the edges brown and become crispy. This specific thermal process is what defines the final texture. Without the browning and crisping, the rice remains a loose, soft porridge that cannot support the weight of the filling. The decisive step is not the assembly, but the interaction between the rice, the cheese, and the oven. The rice is pressed into the parchment-lined baking sheet to form a compact, thin layer. This density is crucial. If the rice is too loose or thick, the heat will dry it out unevenly, resulting in a chewy center or a brittle, broken shell. The cheese plays a secondary but supportive role: it melts, binds the surface of the rice, and aids in the browning process that creates the necessary crunch. The 18-20 minute duration at 180 °C is the window where this change occurs. The cue for readiness is visual and textural: the edges must be browned and crispy. If this state is not reached, the structural integrity of the "roll" fails. Filling and Assembly While the rice cakes bake, the filling is prepared to remain cool and distinct from the hot shell. The filling consists of 80-90 g of lightly salted red fish, 100 g of crab sticks, and a small fresh cucumber, all finely chopped. These are mixed with 120 g of cream cheese to create a cohesive, moist mass. The contrast here is intentional: the hot, dry, crispy rice shell against the cool, soft, creamy filling. The assembly is simple: the filling is placed on the warm, crisp rice disc, and the cake is folded in half like an envelope. This fold relies entirely on the structural strength gained during baking. If the rice cake is undercooked or too thick, it will bend or crack instead of holding the fold. A finish of 1-2 teaspoons of sesame seeds and a side of soy sauce complete the presentation, highlighting the textural difference between the crisp exterior and the soft interior.

headline: Marcos appoints SSS president as DICT secretary
snippet: PRESIDENT Ferdinand Marcos Jr. named Social Security System (SSS) President and CEO Robert Joseph de Claro as the new secretary of the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT). Marcos made the announcement on Tuesday, citing de Claro’s strong background in the digital economy as a qualification for the position. De Claro replaces Henry Aguda, who resigned last week. “He joined the Social Security Commission in January of ’23 and he’s the chair of the Information and Technology Collection Committee in the SSS. He represented SSS on the boards of Union Bank, which is the number one digital bank that we have, and chairman of the board of Union Digital Bank,” Marcos said. In an interview with reporters, de Claro said he will review all the projects, budgets, and procurement at the department. “I assure the public that over the next three months, there should be a clear-cut plan on how we take the ICT to where it should be,” he said. When asked about the ongoing investigation of the “ghost internet” issue — where non-existent free Wi-Fi installation sites were reported — de Claro said the agency plans to have at least 20,000 sites installed nationwide by the end of the year. “I think this year, there’s about 12,000 sites already installed. That is one of our achievements actually, we have 20,000 sites by the end of the year,” he said. “We need the assistance of the providers to ensure that the gadgets installed in the different sites are working properly,” he added. Asked if Aguda should take accountability for the issue, de Claro said the former DICT secretary “did his best to try to find ways and means on how to help provide better technology to the Philippines.”
